usage: I go back to my hometown.
로 marks the direction returned toward
It goes back to how it was.
Returning to a former state, not just a place
I will go back next month.
거예요 future for a planned return
examples: 이제 집에 돌아가요.
I'm going back home now.
The 가 stem swallows the 아 ending, so it's 돌아가요, never 돌아가아요.
너무 피곤해서 호텔로 돌아가고 싶어요.
I'm so tired I want to go back to the hotel.
고 싶어요 adds the wish; 로 points back toward the hotel.
우리 이제 숙소로 돌아갈까요?
Shall we head back to the lodging now?
ㄹ까요 floats a gentle group suggestion.
nuance: 돌아가다 is literally 돌아(turn around) + 가다(go), so it paints you turning back and heading AWAY from the listener toward your origin — home, your country, a former state. The razor-sharp contrast is with 돌아오다(come back): direction is fixed by the speaker's standpoint, exactly like English go vs come, so a tourist phoning home says 한국에 돌아갈 거예요 (going back, away from here), but once landed says 집에 돌아왔어요 (came back). It also means revert: 원래대로 돌아가다 (go back to normal), even 돌아가시다 is the gentle euphemism for passing away, so tread carefully. As a 가다 compound it conjugates regularly and the 가 + 아 contracts to 가요. The English-speaker trap: do not force 에서 on the destination — you return TO a place with 에/로, never 집에서 돌아가요.

mistakes: Saying 집에 돌아와요 when you're talking to someone back home about flying home — from your current spot the motion goes away, so it must be 돌아가요; 돌아오다 is only for motion toward where you are now.
Writing 돌아가아요 by adding the full 아요 ending — the 가 stem already ends in ㅏ, so it contracts to 돌아가요.
Using 에서 for the place you return to (집에서 돌아가요). Return destinations take 에 or 로; 에서 would mean you start FROM the house.

usage: 에서 marks the starting point you leave from
정시에 = on the dot, a timetable collocation
하다 splits so 안 sits between 출발 and 해요
examples: 우리 이제 출발해요!
Let's set off now!
출발 + 하다, and 하 + 아 always fuses to 해, giving 출발해요.
버스가 9시에 출발하니까 서둘러야 해요.
The bus leaves at 9, so we'd better hurry.
니까 gives the reason; time of departure takes 에.
비가 와도 예정대로 출발할 거예요.
Even if it rains, we'll depart as planned.
아도 = even if; 예정대로 = as scheduled.
nuance: 출발하다 is Sino-Korean 出發(출발: 出 go out + 發 set off/shoot) plus 하다, the crisp word for a journey or vehicle SETTING OFF from a starting line. Contrast it with 떠나다(leave): 출발하다 is neutral and logistical, fixed on the departure point and time (기차가 출발하다), so a station announcer uses it; 떠나다 carries the emotional weight of leaving something or someone behind. The starting place takes 에서 (부산에서 출발해요) and the time takes 에 (3시에 출발해요). Because it's a 하다 verb the stem 하 + 아 fuses to 해, so present is 출발해요 and the negative splits as 출발 안 해요. English-speaker pitfall: don't mark the start point with 에 — you depart FROM somewhere, so it's 공항에서 출발해요, and the opposite endpoint verb is 도착하다.

mistakes: Marking the starting place with 에 (공항에 출발해요). The origin you leave from takes 에서; 에 would point at a destination, which belongs to 도착하다.
Saying 출발하지 않아요 / 출발해 안 해요 awkwardly — the clean short negative of a 하다 verb is 출발 안 해요, splitting the noun from 해요.
Treating it as emotional 'leave' for people (친구를 출발했어요). To leave a person or place behind you need 떠나다; 출발하다 is for setting off on a route or schedule.

usage: Arrival point takes 에, never 에서
제시간에 = right on time, a fixed phrase
무사히 (safe and sound) is a warm reassurance collocation
방금 = a moment ago, pairs with the past 했어요
examples: 방금 역에 도착했어요.
I just got to the station.
Arrival point 역 takes 에; 도착 + 하 + 았 → 도착했어요.
역에 도착하면 전화해 주세요.
Call me once you arrive at the station.
면 = when/once; 주세요 makes it a polite request.
길이 막혀서 제시간에 도착 못 해요.
Traffic's bad, so I can't make it on time.
Inability splits as 도착 못 해요 around the noun.
nuance: 도착하다 is Sino-Korean 到着(도착: 到 reach + 着 attach/touch down) plus 하다 — the moment of REACHING and touching a destination. Its mirror is 출발하다(depart), and the key is the particle: you arrive AT a place with 에 (호텔에 도착해요), whereas 출발하다 leaves FROM a place with 에서. Don't confuse it with 들어가다/들어오다(enter): 도착하다 is reaching the destination's threshold, not stepping inside a building. As a 하다 verb, 하 + 아 fuses to 해 (도착해요) and the short negative and inability split the noun off: 도착 안 해요, 도착 못 해요. The classic English-speaker error is copying 'arrive at' as 에서 — 'at' here is the static endpoint 에, so 공항에 도착해요, and 공항에서 도착해요 is wrong.

mistakes: Using 에서 for the arrival point (공항에서 도착했어요) by mapping English 'arrive at'. The destination reached takes 에; 에서 marks a source, which belongs to 출발/떠나다.
Mixing it up with 들어가다 (enter) — 도착하다 means you've reached the place, not that you've walked inside. To go in through the door, use 들어가다.
Forming inability as 못 도착해요 in this set — the natural split-negative for the 하다 verb is 도착 못 해요, keeping 못 right before 해요.

usage: The place left behind takes 을/를, not 에서
I set off on a trip.
여행을 떠나다 = embark on a journey, a set phrase
Carries emotional weight of leaving for good
곁을 떠나다 = leave someone's side, intimate register
examples: 저 내일 떠나요.
I'm leaving tomorrow.
나 + 아 contracts, so it's 떠나요, never 떠나아요.
복잡한 도시를 잠시 떠나고 싶어요.
I want to get away from the busy city for a while.
The place left takes 를; 고 싶어요 adds the wish.
우리 함께 여행을 떠날까요?
Shall we set off on a trip together?
여행을 떠나다 is the idiom for embarking; ㄹ까요 suggests.
nuance: 떠나다 means to LEAVE a place, person, or situation behind, and unlike neutral 출발하다(depart) it carries feeling — separation, finality, the pull of moving on, which is why songs and goodbyes use it (곁을 떠나다 leave someone's side). The dividing line with 출발하다: a train 출발해요 (sets off on schedule) but a person 고향을 떠나요 (leaves home, emotionally). The thing left behind takes the object particle 을/를, not 에서 — this is the big surprise for English speakers, since you'd expect 'leave from'. So it's 한국을 떠나요 (I leave Korea), and 여행을 떠나다 idiomatically means to embark on a trip. It's a native verb; 나 + 아 contracts to 나, giving 떠나요 and past 떠났어요.

mistakes: Marking the place left with 에서 (서울에서 떠나요) on the model of 'leave from'. With 떠나다 the abandoned place is a direct object: 서울을 떠나요.
Swapping in 출발하다 for an emotional or final leaving (가족을 출발했어요). Leaving family/home/a person behind needs 떠나다; 출발하다 is only setting off on a route.
Writing 떠나아요 with the full 아요 ending — the stem 떠나 already ends in ㅏ, so it stays 떠나요 and the past is 떠났어요.

usage: Works for a vehicle halting on its own
발걸음을 멈추다 = stop in one's tracks, set phrase
지 마세요 tells someone not to halt
examples: 차가 갑자기 멈췄어요.
The car stopped all of a sudden.
추 + 어 fuses to 춰, so past is 멈췄어요.
저 앞에서 잠깐 멈춰 주세요.
Please pull over briefly just ahead.
춰 주세요 politely asks the driver to halt.
빨간불이니까 여기서 멈춰야 해요.
It's a red light, so we have to stop here.
니까 gives the reason; 야 해요 = must.
nuance: 멈추다 means coming to a HALT — ceasing motion that was underway — and it covers a person freezing, a car braking, the rain letting up, even a clock stopping (시계가 멈췄어요). The fine contrast is with 서다: 서다 emphasizes the final standing-still snapshot (차가 섰다), while 멈추다 highlights the act of arresting the movement; in daily speech they overlap heavily for vehicles. Keep it apart from 그만두다(quit), which abandons an activity or job permanently — you 멈추다 your steps but 그만두다 your job. It also has a transitive use, to stop something: 울음을 멈추다 (stop crying). It's a regular ㅜ-stem verb, so 추 + 어 contracts to 춰, giving 멈춰요 and past 멈췄어요. Pitfall: don't reach for 그만두다 just to say a moving thing stopped.

mistakes: Using 그만두다 for a halting motion (버스가 그만뒀어요). 그만두다 means to quit/give up an activity; a bus coming to a stop is 버스가 멈췄어요.
Writing 멈추어요 / 멈추었어요 in full — natural speech contracts 추+어 to 춰, so it's 멈춰요 and 멈췄어요.
Assuming it's only intransitive — 멈추다 also takes an object (눈물을 멈추다, stop the tears), so you don't always need a separate causative.

usage: 몸을 움직이다 = get the body moving, exercise nuance
조금씩 (little by little) suits gradual motion
꼼짝 + negative = not budge an inch
Frozen-pose request, e.g. for a photo
examples: 사람이 너무 많아서 못 움직여요.
There are so many people I can't move.
못 + 움직여요 expresses physical inability.
사진 찍을 때 움직이지 마세요.
Don't move while I take the photo.
지 마세요 asks someone to hold still.
짐이 무거우니까 조심히 움직여야 해요.
The luggage is heavy, so move carefully.
조심히 = carefully; 야 해요 = must.
nuance: 움직이다 is the broad word for MOVING or shifting position, and its range is wide: your own body (몸을 움직이다), a crowd inching forward, an object that budges, even an abstract heart being moved (마음이 움직이다 = to be swayed). Contrast it with 이사하다(move house), the Sino-Korean 移徙 word reserved for relocating your home — English 'move' covers both, but Korean splits them, so 'I'm moving next month' is 이사해요, never 움직여요. It also differs from 옮기다(transfer/relocate a thing), which is transitive and deliberate (책상을 옮기다, shift the desk). 움직이다 itself works both intransitively (안 움직여요, it won't move) and transitively (몸을 움직여요). It's a regular 이-stem verb: 이 + 어 fuses to 여, giving 움직여요 and 움직였어요. Pitfall: don't use it for changing residence.

mistakes: Saying 다음 달에 움직여요 for changing homes. Relocating your residence is 이사하다 (이사해요); 움직이다 is physical motion, not moving house.
Confusing it with transitive 옮기다 for shifting a specific object (의자를 움직여 주세요 when you mean 'move it over there'). For deliberately relocating a thing, 옮기다 is more precise.
Writing 움직이어요 in full — the 이 stem plus 어 contracts to 여, so it's 움직여요 and past 움직였어요.

usage: 횡단보도 = crosswalk, the everyday partner noun
무사히 reassures about a risky crossing
examples: 여기서 길을 건너요.
We cross the street here.
너 + 어 contracts, so it's 건너요, never 건너어요.
초록불일 때 길을 건너야 해요.
You must cross when the light is green.
ㄹ 때 = when; 야 해요 = must.
차가 오니까 지금 건너지 마세요.
A car's coming, so don't cross now.
지 마세요 is a polite warning not to cross.
nuance: 건너다 means crossing FROM one side TO the other — a street, a river, a bridge, the sea — picturing the whole traverse from edge to edge. The road or water you cross takes the object particle 을/를 (길을 건너요), which surprises English speakers who expect 'across' to be adverbial. The sharp contrast is with 넘다(go over): 넘다 stresses surmounting a high obstacle or boundary, going OVER a mountain pass, a wall, even a limit (산을 넘다, 한계를 넘다), whereas 건너다 is the flat side-to-side passage of a road or river. There's also the compound 건너가다/건너오다 when you want to add the go/come direction. It's a native verb whose stem 건너 ends in ㅓ, so 너 + 어 contracts to 너, giving 건너요 and past 건넜어요. Pitfall: don't use 넘다 for an ordinary crosswalk.

Using 넘다 for crossing a flat street (길을 넘어요). 넘다 means going over a height or limit; an ordinary road or river is 건너다.
Writing 건너어요 with the full ending — the ㅓ-final stem contracts, so the present is 건너요 and the past is 건넜어요.

usage: I pass in front of the bank.
앞을 지나가다 = pass in front of, with 을
For traffic going by without stopping
examples: 방금 버스가 지나갔어요.
The bus just went by.
지나가 + 았 → 지나갔어요; 가 stem contracts.
잠깐만요, 좀 지나가 주세요.
Excuse me, please let me through.
지나가 주세요 politely asks for room to pass.
이 골목을 지나가면 시장이 나와요.
Go past this alley and you'll hit the market.
면 = if/when; handy for directions.
nuance: 지나가다 is 지나(pass) + 가다(go) — moving PAST a point and continuing on, AWAY from the listener, without stopping; a bus goes by, you slip past someone, a season passes (여름이 지나가다). Distinguish it from plain 지나다, which leans toward time ELAPSING (3년이 지났어요, three years passed) and is less about physical motion through space. Its pair 지나오다 adds the come-this-way direction. The place you pass takes 을/를, often with 앞을 (은행 앞을 지나가요, pass in front of the bank). Figuratively 지나가는 말 means an offhand remark made in passing. As a 가다 compound it's regular and 가 + 았 contracts to 갔, giving past 지나갔어요. Pitfall: for 'three years have passed' don't say 지나가다; that physical-motion verb sounds odd for elapsed time — use 지나다 (지났어요).

Marking the place passed with 에서 (가게에서 지나가요). The spot you go past takes 을/를, frequently 앞을: 가게 앞을 지나가요.
Confusing direction with 지나오다 — 지나가다 moves past and away from you; if something passed and is now coming toward you, use 지나오다.

usage: Also figurative: can't keep pace/catch up
examples: 저 그냥 따라갈게요.
I'll just follow along.
ㄹ게요 states your own intention to tag along.
길을 모르니까 가이드를 따라가야 해요.
I don't know the way, so I have to follow the guide.
Person followed takes 를; 야 해요 = must.
다리가 아파서 빨리 못 따라가요.
My leg hurts, so I can't keep up.
못 따라가다 = can't keep pace, literal or figurative.
nuance: 따라가다 is 따라(along/following) + 가다(go) — going ALONG behind someone or something, moving in the same direction AWAY from the listener; you trail a guide, tag after a friend, or figuratively 'keep up' (못 따라가요, can't keep pace). usage: I take them to the hospital.
I take them along with me.
examples: 저도 그 식당에 좀 데려가 주세요.
Please take me to that restaurant too.
데려가 주세요 asks to be brought along; 에 marks where.
아이를 학교에 데려가요.
I take my child to school.
Person 아이 takes 를, destination 학교 takes 에.
주말에 부모님을 바다에 데려가고 싶어요.
I want to take my parents to the sea this weekend.
데려가다 for people; 가져가다 would be wrong here.
nuance: 데려가다 is 데리다(accompany) + 가다(go) — taking a PERSON or animal along with you, moving AWAY from the listener to another place; you take a child to school, a friend to a restaurant, a dog to the vet. The crucial split is animacy: 데려가다 is ONLY for living beings, while 가져가다 is for objects — English 'take' blurs them, so 'take the kids' is 아이들을 데려가요 but 'take the bags' is 가방을 가져가요. Picking 데려오다 when the motion is away from you — taking someone elsewhere from here is 데려가요; 데려오다 is bringing a person toward your location.

usage: I pack it and take it.
챙겨 가다 = gather up and bring along
도 돼요 asks permission to take
examples: 이거 집에 가져가요.
I'm taking this home.
Object 이거 takes the spot of 을; 가 stem contracts in 가져가요.
비가 오니까 우산을 가져가야 해요.
It's raining, so I should take an umbrella.
Thing 우산 takes 를; 야 해요 = must.
남은 음식은 집에 가져가도 돼요?
Can I take the leftovers home?
도 돼요 politely asks permission.

usage: The object brought takes 을/를 (often dropped casually)
로/에 marks toward the speaker's spot
와 주세요 politely asks someone to bring it
Figurative: 가져오다 = bring about a result
examples: 물 한 잔 가져와요.
Bring a glass of water.
오 + 아 fuses to 와, so it's 가져와요, never 가져오아요.
메뉴판 좀 가져와 주세요.

와 주세요 is the standard polite 'please bring' in a café.
여권을 안 가져와서 걱정이에요.

안 가져오다 negates; 아서 gives the reason.
